terms.register: vōx cōmica: Plaut., Ter.; also Cic. (Rab. Post. 45)
evidence: Ter. Ad. 373: Hem, Dēmea, haud aspexeram tē.
terms.comment: Lewis & Short: surprise in a good or a bad sense, admiration, joy, grief, indignation. The commonest “oh!” of comedy; the manuscripts often confuse it with em (“there!”, see here you are).

evidence: Ter. Ad. 901: Ehem, pater mī, tū hīc erās?
Plaut. Asin. 449b: Ehem, optume. quam dūdum tū advēnistī?
terms.comment: Lewis & Short: “an exclamation of joyful surprise”. The word for “oh, it’s you!”.

evidence: Plaut. Cas. 522b: Oh, nimium scītē scītus es.
terms.comment: Lewis & Short: “for the most various emotions”: surprise, pleasure, sorrow, aversion; repeated, oh oh oh, in lament (Plaut. Capt. 200a).

terms.gloss: oh (with a name, or exclaiming at something)
terms.grammar: with the vocative, or the accusative of exclamation
evidence: Ter. Ad. 790: Ō caelum, ō terra, ō maria Neptūnī!
Cic. Att. 13.52.1: ō hospitem mihi tam gravem!
terms.comment: Not a word on its own: it opens an address or an exclamation.

phrases.latin: Hem, Dēmea, haud aspexeram tē. Quid agitur?
phrases.english: Oh, Demea, I hadn’t seen you. How are things?

phrases.latin: Quid agitur, Aeschine? — Ehem, pater mī, tū hīc erās?
phrases.english: How are you, Aeschinus? — Oh, Dad, you were here?

phrases.latin: Quis hīc loquitur? ehem, tūne hīc erās, mī Phaedria?
phrases.english: Who’s that talking? Oh, was it you here, my Phaedria?
Oh, you’re far too clever by half.

phrases.latin: Ō caelum, ō terra, ō maria Neptūnī!
phrases.english: O heaven, O earth, O seas of Neptune! (mock-tragic: good for a dropped cup)
